items.readable_text:
Content:
When we divide two whole numbers using long division, we often get a remainder. In this lesson, we will learn how to use long division to express the quotient and remainder as a decimal.

Content:
To illustrate, let's compute [MATH: 4 \div 5.] We start by writing down [MATH: 4\div 5] using long division notation:

Content:
| | | [MATH: \,\,0] | / | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: \!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{\color{red}4}] | |

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \color{red}4] is less than the divisor [MATH: 5.] But we can proceed further by adding a [MATH: \color{blue}0] after the decimal point in the dividend. We also add a decimal point in the quotient, as shown below:

Content:
| | | [MATH: \,0 {\bbox[2pt, lightgray]{\color{blue}.}}] | / | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: \!\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{{\color{red}4} {\bbox[2pt, lightgray]{\color{blue}.}} {\color{blue}0}}] | |

Content:
Now we complete the division, as usual, stopping once we obtain a remainder of [MATH: 0\mathbin{:}]

Content:
| | | [MATH: \,0 {\,.\,} 8] | / | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: \!\!\require{enclose}\enclose{longdiv}{4 {\, . \,} 0 }] | / | [MATH: -\!\!\!\!\!] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 0] | / | | | [MATH: \fbox{0}] | |

Content:
Therefore,
[MATH: 4 \div 5 = 0.8\,.]
